content:
cslib#615 contains an example of how we can do NTM based on the libraries we already have, and the necessary theory to fix to EpsilonNA in terms of saturated multistep transitions. (Fixing the bug that sometimes epsilonNA wouldn't accept an empty string when it should.)

This is what's ready that we discussed today, @chris477, @Samuel Schlesinger, @Chris Henson, @Shreyas Srinivas.

It would be nice if we could re-use the formalism and especially also the tools and results from the formalism. I haven't had a deep look at the formalism. I understand that it is able to capture many different kinds of automata and computations, but my fear is that the tools it provides does not outweigh the complications it adds on top of something that in the end is "just" a relation, and all we need to be able to express is reachability in at most t steps in this graph.
Maybe you could prove some simple results using this definition of NTM? The fact that all regular languages can be accepted in constant space for example should be easy to do if they use the same formalism. Then there are things like a bound on the number of configurations reachable in t steps or something more advanced like the fact that a machine that uses at most s space can take at most an exponential number of steps in s (if it terminates).
The advantage of this formalism is that many facts about nondeterministic machines directly translate to deterministic machines.

@Fabrizio Montesi a concrete implementation question here : Is there a reason you prefer to label your transitions with these three kinds of labels? Why not just declare an inductive type of all possible transitions?

Concretely, couldn't we split the transition into steps of read, write, move, etc. Here's my reasoning:

When we write TMs we say things like : "Read the current cell, change state to s, keep reading until some state + cell combo is reached, move to the next cell and then write such and such character". In a sense these are the unit operations of a TM in terms of which all transition functions are built and specified. Why not go for this more primitive notion (like mathlib's stack based TM)? I think it will be easier to program TMs using lean functions in this way. Thus a "run" of a TM is essentially this sequence of operations.

I initially implemented this locally for my cslib PR as merely an oracle, but I think it can be just how we write transition functions in the first place. Happy to share code if you would like to see it, but it's from a different repository.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Fabrizio Montesi a concrete implementation question here : Is there a reason you prefer to label your transitions with these three kinds of labels? Why not just declare an inductive type of all possible transitions?

I wanted to allow the combo 'reading a char, writing a char, and moving the head' to count as a single unit of work. If, instead, we want each of these three operations to count as one independent unit of work, then we can (as you suggest, I think) make TrLabel an inductive with the four options read, write, move the head, or do nothing.
I think the triple is quite clean. Especially always having to store the read symbol in the state can be quite annoying.
@chris477 re your first mesg: I think a natural good test would be to create a function that transforms an N(F)A into an NTM and then prove language equivalence. Sounds good?
If adding another state is already annoying in this model then it’s not the right model :sweat_smile:

You gotta compare it with doing it without this model, which would likely be even more annoying.
Automata and TMs have different accepting conditions so that needs to be mapped. It's the underlying transition machinery that is shared, so the advantage is more the fact that we deal with only an API and can reuse its theorems on both sides (NA and its NTM translation).

Fabrizio Montesi said:

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Fabrizio Montesi a concrete implementation question here : Is there a reason you prefer to label your transitions with these three kinds of labels? Why not just declare an inductive type of all possible transitions?

I wanted to allow the combo 'reading a char, writing a char, and moving the head' to count as a single unit of work. If, instead, we want each of these three operations to count as one independent unit of work, then we can (as you suggest, I think) make TrLabel an inductive with the four options read, write, move the head, or do nothing.

Btw, I wanted it to stick to the pen and paper presentations I've seen. Having the inductive would indeed be simpler, so if we can agree that each read/write/move operation should count as work in isolation, then I'd be happy to make the change.
As a concrete example, it'd be impossible to read a symbol and change it on the tape in a single step in the reduction semantics of configurations.

In the end this all does not matter. There are textbook definitions of both styles. It all boils down to proof ergonomics. And then again: at least i don’t plan to use TMs much for upper bounds. The only point I plan to construct a tm explicitly is in the equivalence proof :sweat_smile:
The point about halting: I think it’s more convenient if you only have to prove that a halting configuration is reachable in t steps and not also that it’s the first.

Fabrizio Montesi said:

I wanted to allow the combo 'reading a char, writing a char, and moving the head' to count as a single unit of work. If, instead, we want each of these three operations to count as one independent unit of work, then we can (as you suggest, I think) make TrLabel an inductive with the four options read, write, move the head, or do nothing.

...
Btw, I wanted it to stick to the pen and paper presentations I've seen. Having the inductive would indeed be simpler, so if we can agree that each read/write/move operation should count as work in isolation, then I'd be happy to make the change.

The problem with any textbook definition is that textbooks stop using them precisely after the first two or three chapters, and I have definitely seen papers count reads and writes separately. So I am okay with counting reads, writes etc separately since we do need to keep track of writes anyway for at least some of the definitions of complexity classes. This only makes a small constant factor difference in time complexity, and no difference in space complexity. This is a small tradeoff to achieve significant gains in convenience of writing TMs

I've encountered lots of interesting things working on the 'simple' proof that a TM can implement an (epsilon)NFA. Some of the choices that come out of that, I think, we need to discuss (perhaps at the upcoming CSLib General Meeting).

In the meantime I've put the less controversial bits not related to NTM in a separate PR, which is more urgent since that includes fixes, see #CSLib: PR reviews > #625: Saturated multistep transitions and derived work.
Oh that’s interesting, I would love to hear about them! The next meeting I can attend is on the 23rd - but I also don’t have much time for offline discussions until then.
